title: Bar Barra Peñasco / Estudio CR
text:
Bar Barra Peñasco / Estudio CR

Barra Peñasco is a high-end bar inside the Rosewood Mandarina Hotel in the Riviera Nayarit. Perched on a cliffside between the canopy of white fig trees and palms, it faces the Pacific Ocean. The project responds to the site's unique conditions through an open architecture that accompanies different moments of hospitality: arriving, taking a seat, sharing a drink, and lingering as the sunset transforms the horizon and music extends the experience into the night. Its mixology menu, inspired by the four elements and Náyeri and Wixárika traditions, dialogues with this natural setting.

title: Oslo Houses / Nommo Arquitetos
text:
Oslo Houses / Nommo Arquitetos

Color does not belong to things; it does not exist on its own, but rather emerges from the encounter between light, matter, and the human gaze. It is a perception, a sensory experience capable of changing how we read the world and space. This capability, as Le Corbusier recognized, is a tool of architecture, where polychromy can shift planes in depth and transform the perception of volumes.

title: Clarke House / Austin Maynard Architects
text:
Clarke House / Austin Maynard Architects

title: Guilliers School Restaurant / eeun architecure
text:
Guilliers School Restaurant / eeun architecure

The Guilliers School Restaurant transforms a former commercial building into a municipal facility serving the two primary schools of the village. Rather than extending urban development onto new land, the project demonstrates how an ordinary existing building can become a generous public space through careful transformation. The ambition was not only to create a functional school restaurant for 90 children, but also to reveal the qualities already present in the existing structure while significantly reducing the environmental impact of construction.

title: Architecture as a Social Practice: Lessons from Ammodo Architecture Days
text:
Architecture as a Social Practice: Lessons from Ammodo Architecture Days

What connects a cooperative housing development in Barcelona, a cultural institution hosted in an unfinished concrete structure in Accra, and a floating festival platform in the Peruvian Amazon? Despite their unique geographic and social contexts, these projects encourage an understanding of architecture that extends beyond the construction of buildings. Through collective housing, adaptive reuse, participatory design processes, and community-led initiatives, they demonstrate how architectural practice creates opportunities for communities to shape their built environments.

title: "Any User of a Space Is Also Its Producer": In Conversation With Vyjayanthi Rao at the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial
text:
"Any User of a Space Is Also Its Producer": In Conversation With Vyjayanthi Rao at the 2026 Sharjah Architecture Triennial

The third edition of the Sharjah Architecture Triennial (SAT03), titled Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures, opened on November 14, 2026, and will run until April 14, 2027, across Sharjah, United Arab Emirates. Curated by anthropologist Vyjayanthi Rao and Associate Curator Tau Tavengwa, the edition brings together different forms of spatial knowledge and practice, considering how collective life is shaped through interactions, relationships, and negotiations. During the Triennial's opening week, ArchDaily's Editor-in-Chief Christele Harrouk spoke with Rao about the thinking behind this curatorial direction, the relationship between architecture and civic infrastructure, and the potential of architectural practice to engage with broader social and political conditions.

title: Geneo / Serie Architects + Multiply Architects + Surbana Jurong
text:
Geneo / Serie Architects + Multiply Architects + Surbana Jurong

Designed to meet the changing needs of the life sciences and technology sectors, Geneo introduces a new generation of science park development. It incorporates a series of innovations responding to the changing needs of the science park typology, laboratory and workplace environment with curated social, wellness and community spaces, fostering greater collaboration, knowledge exchange within a vibrant work-live-play environment.

title: A Guide to Urban Resilience Against El Niño and BIG's Refugee City Masterplan: This Week’s Review
text:
A Guide to Urban Resilience Against El Niño and BIG's Refugee City Masterplan: This Week’s Review

Two timely themes ran through this week's news: the integration of inherited and new elements in restoration and renovation projects at both large and small scales, and the idea of an architecture reconciled with the environment. The latter concept is borrowed from the Ambasz–MoMA Annual Prize, established to recognize exemplary projects that repair the relationship between architecture and nature and provide financial support for environmental action. Another form of support for such action was presented this week in a guide by UN-Habitat and ICPAC, which helps local governments organize disaster management in response to expected flooding caused by the El Niño climate phenomenon. In our radar, a controversial design by BIG for refugee settlements in Uganda raises questions; the US Green Building Council introduces new tools for architectural decarbonization through a new guide; and a project by OODA in Portugal reinforces the trend of transforming sports venues into multifunctional spaces for public use.

title: The Architecture of Distance: Encountering Wildlife at Shomari Wild Reserve
text:
The Architecture of Distance: Encountering Wildlife at Shomari Wild Reserve

What does it mean to encounter another living subject through architecture? The experience of observing wildlife is often understood in terms of proximity: how close we can get, how clearly we can see, and how much of an animal's world we are able to enter. Yet the desire to encounter wildlife also depends on maintaining a distance. Animals inhabit environments that are not organized around human presence, and their experience of these environments cannot be fully understood from the observer's position. Between the desire to see and the need to preserve lies a more complicated relationship, one that architecture is increasingly required to negotiate.

title: Villa in Nishinokyo / ALIANA ARCHITECTS
text:
Villa in Nishinokyo / ALIANA ARCHITECTS

The site is located in Nishinokyo-Enmachi, Kyoto. The plot measures a mere 17 *tsubo* (approx. 56 square meters), forming a long, narrow "eel's bed" shape—4 meters wide and 14 meters deep. Here, we constructed a small house that combines warehouse functionality with a full suite of residential amenities for living and sleeping.

title: The Outpost Cabin / Ample
text:
The Outpost Cabin / Ample

Located at Charnley River Station in the remote Kimberley region of Western Australia, The Outpost is a collection of eight architecturally designed accommodation buildings developed by Ample for Australian Wildlife Conservancy (AWC). Designed in partnership with Agents of Architecture, with interiors by Unearthed Interiors, the project explores how off-site construction can deliver considered architecture in one of Australia's most isolated and environmentally significant landscapes.

title: When Does Shipping Container Architecture Make Sense?
text:
When Does Shipping Container Architecture Make Sense?

Using shipping containers as the basis for a structure—also known as "cargotecture"—seems like a simple approach to building. Perhaps deceptively so. While it's true that containers are a quick, cost-effective, and often low-effort building material, and that they're durable and customizable, container conversions also bring their challenges. Without careful planning, the build process can be painful and the results underwhelming.

title: Icon Place Shibakoen Renovation / Gensler + Rockwell Group
text:
Icon Place Shibakoen Renovation / Gensler + Rockwell Group

Gensler has renovated a 30-year-old office building in Tokyo's Shibakoen district, repositioning it as ICON PLACE Shibakoen, a hybrid building that combines offices, residences, and publicly accessible open space. The area sits close to Tokyo Tower, with cherry blossom-lined streets and a long history alongside green space, and the renovation was designed to connect the building more closely to that setting.

title: The Balcony of Guápulo / IWI Studio
text:
The Balcony of Guápulo / IWI Studio

The project consists of the expansion of a house located in the Guápulo valley in Quito. The intervention transforms a previously inaccessible roof into a new livable space open to the landscape—a domestic balcony overlooking the valley—incorporating a bedroom, a study, and a bathroom within a single, continuous space.

title: Kaybe Tulum - Multisensorial Park / Arquitectura Mixta
text:
Kaybe Tulum - Multisensorial Park / Arquitectura Mixta

Kaybé Multisensory Park is an immersive architectural experience that explores the relationship between nature, energy, and human perception through a sequence of sculptural bamboo structures set within the tropical jungle of Tulum.

title: Place des Montréalaises / Lemay + Angela Silver + AtkinsRéalis
text:
Place des Montréalaises / Lemay + Angela Silver + AtkinsRéalis

Place des Montréalaises: A Monumental Gesture Inscribing Women's Memory at the Heart of a City
Place des Montréalaises is reshaping Montreal's civic and tourist heart by covering a sunken expressway with a vibrant esplanade. Designed by Lemay in collaboration with artist Angela Silver and the engineering team at AtkinsRéalis, this major intervention connects Old Montreal to downtown and inscribes the memory of exceptional women in the urban landscape.

title: Preistoriche Green Lodge  / Studio Apostoli
text:
Preistoriche Green Lodge / Studio Apostoli

An eco-friendly approach to hospitality, in full respect of the region and its preexisting elements: the new Green Lodges of the Terme Preistoriche Resort & Spa in Montegrotto Terme (PD), designed by Studio Apostoli, is meant to be a manifesto of zero-emission wellness hospitality. Seven suites are incorporated into four wooden stilted structures and interconnected through a raised system of ramps, walkways, and accessible terraces. They also include a historically preserved villa, the eighth and most extensive offering within this entrepreneurial endeavor. 160 micro piles support the new constructions and outdoor spaces, preserving the roots of the age-old trees. Alberto Apostoli, the founder of the Verona-based studio responsible for the development, meticulously mapped these trees before outlining any project proposals.

title: Renovation and Extension of La Beaujoire Nursery and Primary School in Nantes / Dominique Coulon & associés
text:
Renovation and Extension of La Beaujoire Nursery and Primary School in Nantes / Dominique Coulon & associés

To develop its neighbourhoods, the city of Nantes decided to build seven new primary schools and renovate 27 of its existing ones. The city entrusted Dominique Coulon & associés with the task of revamping two of them.

title: Call for Entries: The New Heart of Kraaiennest with OBA Next (Amsterdam)
text:
Call for Entries: The New Heart of Kraaiennest with OBA Next (Amsterdam)

The City of Amsterdam is holding an international design competition for the project ‘The New Heart of Kraaiennest with OBA Next’. The purpose of the procurement procedure is to select a design team. The assignment calls for a cohesive design addressing the public realm, civic and community facilities, socioeconomic growth, and the spatial integration of the housing programme. Essential to the assignment is the integration of urban design, landscape, architecture and socioeconomic value.

The full programme for the competition comprises the following spatial components:
• OBA Next library
• Youth centre
• Huis van de Wijk
• Rehearsal space
• Complementary neighbourhood programme
• Housing and facilities

title: Mapping Memory: Reconstructing Architecture Beyond Physical Evidence
text:
Mapping Memory: Reconstructing Architecture Beyond Physical Evidence

How do you remember the dimensions of a room you could barely see? Perhaps through the distance between footsteps, the sound of a door closing, or the way an echo travels down a corridor. For someone who has been denied the ability to see or move freely through a space, these fragments may be the only record of its architecture.

title: Pod for Happiness / Craft Narrative
text:
Pod for Happiness / Craft Narrative

In the small village of Hignigada near Baramati, Maharashtra, a young village head approached us to build an outdoor play area for school children. The school campus had a large playground divided by an avenue of seven trees, with classrooms arranged along the perimeter. Villagers fondly shared how they enjoyed evening walks and sitting under the trees. Inspired by this connection to nature & community space, we designed the play area around the banyan tree, making it the centerpiece of the insert.

title: Send the Firefighters to the Fires
text:
Send the Firefighters to the Fires

Send the firefighters to the fires

Enterprise software keeps forgetting a century of good advice about what deserves our attention.

If a user’s job is to fix what’s broken, the screen should show what’s broken first. Sounds pretty obvious. It’s also not new. Frederick Taylor argued for it in 1903. Xerox PARC designed for it in the ’90s. Industrial control rooms wrote it into a standard. Yet enterprise software keeps forgetting this.

Imagine a fire department that dispatches trucks in the order houses were built. Or by date last renovated. Every house gets a visit eventually, and some of them happen to be on fire. That’s pretty absurd, right? Yet I’ve seen the equivalent more times than I care to remember.

A lot of enterprise work boils down to one job: here’s a collection of things, some of them have problems, go fix the problems. Devices out of compliance. Certificates about to expire. Invoices that failed to reconcile. Tickets breaching SLA. The KPI is simply “issues resolved.”

The UI has one job: get the user to the fires and hand them the hose.

So how did we forget? Not because the ideas are hard. Enterprise software just has a habit of designing for everyone except the person actually using it. It’s designing for the buyer in the demo, for the team racing to ship, for the data model that sorts things for free. None of them pay for it. But the user does, every shift, one scroll at a time.

Start with the job

Clayton Christensen had a simple idea: people don’t buy products for their features. They hire them to get a job done. It’s now known as Jobs to Be Done, or JTBD (Christensen et al., 2016; open-access overview). In enterprise triage, the job is about as plain as it gets: fix what’s broken. Finding it should be the product’s job.

So why do so many screens ignore this? Here’s the pattern I see over and over again. A screen lists 400 objects, and twelve need attention. They’re scattered somewhere between page 3 and page 17. It’s Where’s Waldo, except Waldo is a production outage.

Sometimes there’s a status column. Maybe a small red pill, sitting politely in column six of a list sorted by anything but what matters. A human can work out which items are broken. But the interface is acting obtuse and unhelpful.

Consider the following twenty services. I’ll keep coming back to them.

Before: 20 rows, sorted by last updated, every column visible

After: focus on the fires

In the first table, the two critical services sit in rows sixteen and nineteen, and nothing calls them critical. You have to cross-reference Health and Tier yourself: search-index is only Degraded, but it’s Tier 1; mail-relay is Failing, but it’s Tier 3. Meanwhile, Uptime reads 99.92% for payments-gw, which is failing right now. The fires-first view does that math for you. Same data, different job.

Now imagine hearing that table instead. If the headers are marked up properly, a screen reader announces which column you’re in as you move through it (W3C, F91). So a screen reader user can walk down the Health column one cell at a time. That’s still twenty announcements to find six problems, plus a hop to the Tier column for each one. And that’s the best case: many enterprise data grids are built from divs, virtualized, or paginated, and those shortcuts break. Many enterprises don’t hire people who can build accessible tables (Brad Frost calls them front-of-the-front-end developers), but that’s another story. For every column of noise we leave in, someone has to sit through it.

None of this is malicious. Nobody in the review said “hey, let’s bury the critical issues!” The order happened by default, because nobody dug into the JTBD.

The table as a design cop-out

Bad sort order is an outcome of enterprise’s unfortunate love affair with the table as a magic bullet.

The reasoning goes: we don’t know exactly what users want, so let’s give them all the data and let them search, filter, and sort. It sounds like giving users control. In reality, it’s an abdication.

Those are tools for exploring and hunting: browsing to see what’s there, or tracking down something you know exists. But when they become the main interface for task work, the product team has handed its job to the user. Every session, someone sorts by health, scrolls past the Passing rows, cross-checks the tier, and finds payments-gw. Again. Multiply that by every user, every day. That’s triage the product could have done once.

At some point, some smarty-pants will suggest saved filters: let users build and save their own “To-dos” view (health is failing, sorted by tier). Problem solved, right? Not quite! That’s a workaround stacked on the cop-out. Users end up designing the default screen for you because you shipped the wrong one.

Why smart teams keep doing this

To be fair, the people shipping these screens aren’t careless. The forces pushing them toward the table are real, and a lot of them trace back to one thing: in sales-led enterprise software, the buyer isn’t the user.

Jason Lemkin said it bluntly back in 2012: “you, the end user, aren’t the customer for most true enterprise software” (Lemkin, SaaStr). A year later, Martin Eriksson made the same distinction for product managers: “the user and the purchaser are different people with different needs” (Eriksson, Mind the Product).

The buyer’s worst case is a boring demo. The user’s worst case is an outage with their name on it. Guess who the screen gets designed for. Not every lazy sort comes from sales, but a sales-led motion makes lazy sorts easier to ship and harder to undo.

Defaults feel safe. Every record has a created_at and an updated_at, so sorting by them is free. “Severity” doesn’t exist until someone designs it. Meanwhile, stakeholders worry that if healthy items aren’t visible, users will assume they’re missing, and on an RFP checklist, a hidden column might as well not exist. So everything stays on screen.

Nobody talks to each other. Taiichi Ohno’s 5 Whys only works if you can reach the person with the answer. In enterprise, there are too many layers between the people willing to ask and the people able to answer. The only two people reliably talking are the salesperson and the buyer. The salesperson is paid for the close, and asking why five times only gets in the way. Conway’s law predicts the result: systems mirror how their makers communicate. A neutral sort is what that silence looks like on screen.

“Ask ‘why’ five times about every matter.”
 — Taiichi Ohno, Toyota

Dashboards are built for the demo. People love dashboards that look like command centers in movies. Walls of screens! Scrolling numbers! Blinking maps! Stephen Few was criticizing exactly this two decades ago, arguing that dashboards should support real-time situation awareness for decision making, not impress the room (Few, 2007; Information Dashboard Design, 2006). Density still wins sales calls, which is the sales motion showing up in the UI. Developers and PMs love it too: every widget and column is a feature someone built.

Tables are cheap and familiar. Every component library ships one, and every IC has built a dozen, so it’s what everyone reaches for first. Inline editing is one prop away, so someone will eventually float turning every cell into a form field. Cheap to build, expensive to use.

Notice what these have in common? Each one optimizes for the team’s comfort or the buyer’s first impression, not the user’s job. The table can never be wrong, because it never commits to anything.

Tables aren’t the enemy

To be clear, I’m not anti-table. Reporting, analysis, and bulk admin are table work. User questions can change week to week, and pinning them down takes the kind of conversations we’ve already seen are rare. Designing for that is tough, so a flexible table is an honest answer.

The line I draw is this: open-ended questions need flexible tables. Known jobs need opinionated ones.

Yet sometimes the best table is the one you don’t build! Think about what people actually do with a big table, and where that work belongs:

  • Slice and pivot? Let them export to (or integrate with) the BI tools they already know.
  • Report up to leadership? Send a scheduled summary, not a screenshot of 400 rows.
  • Reconcile against another system? That’s an integration or an API. Please don’t subject a human being to comparing two systems row by row.
  • Hand evidence to auditors? Send an export instead of buying them a seat, which only gets them a login they’ll barely use, to a worse BI tool.

Excel, Tableau, and Power BI are established, they’re good at analysis, and your users already know them. Your product doesn’t need to compete. Just keep the fires list live and in-app.

So the question isn’t table or no table. It’s what goes in it, and in what order. If you can write the user’s job in one sentence, and “resolve the issues” is that sentence, you know enough to decide: fires first, ranked by severity, healthy rows summarized. A table sorted by last updated with every row at equal weight is just an inventory. It tells users what exists, not what needs their attention.

Management by exception, a century later

One of my core design principles fits in four words: no news is good news. I didn’t invent it. In 1903, Frederick Taylor called it the exception principle: a manager shouldn’t be swamped with every report, only with what deviates from the standard (Taylor, Shop Management).

“The manager should receive only condensed, summarized, and invariably comparative reports.”
 — Frederick Winslow Taylor, Shop Management (1903)

Swap “manager” for “user” and it’s a design brief. There’s no reason to emphasize what’s working. Working is the expected state; it’s what the customer pays for. But there’s every reason to emphasize what isn’t, because that’s the only part that needs a human.

Every pixel that gives a healthy object the same weight as a broken one is friction against the KPI. If the metric is issues resolved, a screen that hides issues isn’t neutral. It’s working against the business. And noise isn’t just visual. For a screen reader user, it’s time.

So design as if the user’s job performance depends on your decisions. Because it does! When issues slip through the cracks, nobody blames the designer who picked the default sort. They blame the user who didn’t spot payments-gw in time. They inherit our defaults, our clutter, and our shallow thinking, and they’re the ones who get penalized for it.

That’s the bar. It’s not “does it follow the design system” or “did stakeholders sign off.” It’s “does this make the person using it better at their job?”

What control rooms already know

Ironically, real control rooms don’t look like the movies. In refineries and power plants, operator screens are guided by the ISA-101 standard for industrial interfaces (ISA, 2015), which builds on the high-performance HMI work of Bill Hollifield and colleagues (The High Performance HMI Handbook). Normal operation stays gray and calm. Color is saved for when something’s wrong.

https://medium.com/media/3a2b27bedfc398539b462d0027464e6c/href

The unsexy truth is that sometimes, that’s all a dashboard needs to be: a prioritized list of what’s on fire and the means to put it out, not a bunch of widgets fighting for the user’s attention. Many may not like it, but that’s what peak performance looks like. Operators knew it long before enterprise SaaS did.

Silence has to be earned

Here’s a fair objection: users need reassurance. If I only show problems, how does anybody know the rest is fine?

Sure, Jakob Nielsen’s first usability heuristic covers it. Systems should keep users informed about what is going on, through appropriate feedback within reasonable time (Harley, NN/g). No news is only good news if the silence is trustworthy. An empty screen could mean everything is healthy, or that the sync broke an hour ago. If users can’t tell the difference, they’ll go back to scanning the full table.

So design the quiet state as deliberately as the loud one. Don’t list the healthy items. Summarize them with confidence.

Just a count, a timestamp, and a way to dig deeper. You’re still reporting the good news. You’re just not giving it top billing.

Mark Weiser and John Seely Brown described this balance in 1995 as calm technology: information that sits in the periphery of our attention and moves to the center only when it matters (Weiser and Brown, 1995). In their words, the periphery is “informing without overburdening.” That’s the quiet state. It gives users permission to stop looking. Giving users their time back might be the most underrated thing an enterprise tool can offer.

What fires-first actually looks like

A fires-first approach isn’t just the same table with a different sort. Here’s what separates it, with credit where it’s due.

  • Severity, not just status. A small fire next to a gas station beats a big one in an empty lot. An expired certificate on payments-gw outranks one on a test server, even if both say “Failing.” Health tells you what broke. Tier tells you how much it matters. Severity needs both. Remember that severity doesn’t exist until someone designs it? This is what designing it looks like.
  • Urgency and importance are separate axes. The idea is usually traced to a 1954 Eisenhower speech, and Stephen Covey, A. Roger Merrill, and Rebecca Merrill turned it into four quadrants in First Things First (Hoang, Rework). Plot issues on that matrix, and users can make meaningful choices about what to fix now, schedule, delegate, or snooze.
  • Lead straight into investigation. Fires seldom have a one-click fix. The real job is usually figuring out what went wrong, so each item should invite investigation.
  • Notify, so nobody has to watch. People have better things to do than babysit your app. When payments-gw catches fire, tell the person who can fix it, wherever they already work: email, Slack, Teams. The fires list is where they go to act, not where they sit and wait.
  • Restraint on alerts. Healthcare has studied the opposite failure for years. When clinicians are flooded with warnings, they become desensitized and start overriding the critical ones along with the trivial ones (AHRQ PSNet, “Alert Fatigue”). If 300 of 400 items say “Warning,” your users will do the same. A severity model that can’t say “this doesn’t matter now” isn’t a severity model.
  • Let users snooze. Some fires can’t be fought today: a vendor hasn’t replied, or the fix needs a maintenance window. Snoozing dials down the noise without pretending the issue is solved, and it comes back on schedule.
  • Resolution is visible. When a fire goes out, it leaves the list and the count drops. That feedback loop makes the KPI real to the person doing the work.
  • Everything is still one click away. The full table, healthy rows included, for the audit, the export, and the curious.
“I have two kinds of problems, the urgent and the important.”
— Dwight D. Eisenhower, quoting J. Roscoe Miller, 1954

The top-right quadrant leads the fires list. Everything else still has a home.

Not sure where to start? Watch how users triage today: what they sort by, what they scroll past, what they export. Your users have already mentally drafted the spec.

Dispatch, not census

A census counts everyone equally. That’s its job. A dispatch center decides who needs help first and sends people there.

Most enterprise dashboards are built like a census: complete, neutral, accurate. And no help to someone whose job is putting out the fires.

Taylor got there in 1903. Weiser and Brown in 1995. Few in 2006. The ISA-101 committee in 2015. Same direction, a century apart. The knowledge isn’t missing. What’s missing is defining what “on fire” means, ranking it, designing the quiet state, and wiring up the notifications.

Do the extra work so your users don’t have to. That’s the job.

title: If AI works from anywhere, why are we commuting to watch it?
text:
If AI works from anywhere, why are we commuting to watch it?

Companies say it’s about collaboration. That’s garbage. The reality is a room full of people in headphones, doing alone what they could’ve done at home.

Alexa von Tobel, who runs an early-stage fund and has backed a long list of founders, posted a small, honest question. She hadn’t been pitched a single remote-only company in six months, and she wanted to know if anyone else was seeing it.

The replies were a mix. A few pushed back. One said she had landed a remote role just fine and that nobody had to pitch her anything. Another figured the remote crowd was mostly off building their own companies now.

The reply that stuck with me came from a CEO, who said being fully remote would be harder, and less fun. It resonated because he is half right. Something real does get lost when everyone is scattered. He is just wrong about what fixes it.

What I haven’t seen is anyone ask what should be the obvious question. If the office is winning, what exactly is it “winning” people back to do?

This matters more than it used to, because the thing we always said the office was for has left the building (pun intended). We told ourselves we showed up every day to get the work done together. The making, the producing, the actual output. You went to the office because that was where the work physically got made, and it got made faster with everyone in one place.

Thomas Allen measured the reason decades ago at MIT. The closer two people sit, the more they actually talk, and past about fifty feet the conversation falls off a cliff.

Proximity was the whole point. The commute bought you that.

The work doesn’t live there anymore. It runs on its own now, in the cloud, whether you are at your desk or asleep. Gartner expects forty percent of business software to have agents built into it by the end of 2026, up from under five percent a year earlier.

Offices may still exist, but perhaps we lost the reason for them.

My position is simple, even if the fight over it refuses to be. The office isn’t dead, but it shouldn’t be mandatory. It’s worth protecting for the handful of things people can only do well together, the ones AI can’t touch. Instead it’s being forced on everyone for the work that no longer needs a building at all.

The work left the building

The founders von Tobel is funding are increasingly building agents that do the production themselves. Y Combinator’s recent cohorts are full of companies whose entire pitch is autonomous software that writes, tests, and ships code with a human barely touching it, and the firm’s own partners say AI has collapsed the cost of producing software by a factor of ten to a hundred.

This is not a forecast. It already shows up in who has a job. Erik Brynjolfsson and his colleagues at Stanford’s Digital Economy Lab tracked real payroll data and found that employment for workers aged twenty-two to twenty-five in the most AI-exposed jobs sits about nineteen percent below where it should be, while their older colleagues are fine.

The gap is coming from companies not hiring junior team members, because AI is doing the checkable, process-heavy tasks that used to justify an entry-level seat. You know, the production work, the stuff we all started our careers doing.

It is not only software. Anthropic, looking at how its own models actually get used, found that coding is the single biggest category, and that while most use still has AI working alongside a person, a large and growing share, more than four in ten interactions, is now the model doing the task outright rather than assisting.

The line between the two is blurry, but it is clearly moving in one direction.

Designers feel it and say so. Francisco Barrera Aros points out that AI has swallowed the how of building an interface and is coming for the what, which is why job boards have started sprouting roles like AI Product Designer that nobody could have described two years ago.

AI took over the task of doing the work. The deciding, however, is still yours, and the deciding is where the money is.

Let’s look at what that leaves for the purpose of an office. For a century it was where the production happened, because production needed people in one spot with the files, the tools, and each other. Take that out, hand it to the agents, and the physical building becomes a very expensive room you commute to in order to do work that could happen anywhere.

Which should, by any reasonable prediction, empty the place out.

We all remember 2020, right? The pandemic sent nearly everyone home at once. Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom, and Steven Davis called it a mass social experiment in working from home, with Americans doing roughly half of all paid hours from home through most of 2020, up from about five percent before.

The floors we were told could never go dark went dark, and the striking part, in their data, is how many people were surprised they could do the job from home at all. The mandates coming down treat remote work as an unproven indulgence, when we have years of evidence that most of the job travels. The question should be which parts don’t work and why not?

So everyone scattered, right?

Obviously, work is more portable than it has ever been, but the freer people are to work anywhere, the more they actually want to be together.

Y Combinator, which has funded a good chunk of the companies building these agents, spent years running its batches remotely, and in those years its founders were scattered all over the map. Then it brought the program back in person, in San Francisco, and the founders came right back with it. The trend is easy to see in YC’s own public directory, which one analysis tracked batch by batch.

When the program went remote, barely a quarter of companies listed San Francisco as home. Once it came back in person, that climbed past three quarters, and a chunk of those founders kept choosing the city even after the three months ended and nothing required them to stay. The same batches are stuffed with startups whose product is autonomous software.

The people automating the production hardest are also the people most determined to sit in the same zip code while they do it.

This is one contender to define whole AI era, at least for the workforce. Gensler’s global survey found that the workers most embedded in AI are also the most collaborative and the most drawn to the office, which is the reverse of the lonely-robot future everyone predicted.

As AI takes more of the solo production, the human collaboration it can’t do becomes a scarce, valuable thing, and the people who live in these tools feel the pull toward the room where that still happens.

If the office were really about the work, this is backwards. These founders have built, and are selling, the exact tools that make location irrelevant. They could run these companies from anywhere, and they tell you so with a straight face in the pitch deck. Then they sign a lease three blocks from each other.

The clustering is telling you something that a pitch deck won’t. Whatever they are gathering for, it is not the production, because they already shipped the production to the cloud. It is the other thing.

There is real research on what that other thing is. Daniel Carmody, Martina Mazzarello, Paolo Santi and their colleagues at MIT’s Senseable City Lab studied what happened to people’s networks when everyone went remote, and found that distance measurably starved the weak ties, the loose connections that only form when people share a space. Weak ties are the people you don’t work with closely, the person two teams over, the one you only ever talk to because you both happened to be refilling coffee.

Mark Granovetter named their importance decades ago, in the work that gave us the phrase. The loose connections, not the close ones, are where new information and unlikely ideas actually travel. They are also the first thing to die when everyone is a tile on a screen, because nobody schedules a video call with the person two teams over for no reason.

That is what the founders are re-clustering to get back. Not the work. The accidental stuff around the work. The collisions you cannot put on a calendar, which turn out to be the one thing the agents can’t do for you and the screen can’t give you either.

The office we actually built

Stroll into a lot of these offices and look at what is actually happening.

Rows of people who commuted in to sit at a desk and type into a chatbot. Four people at four screens running four separate conversations with four separate AIs, in the same room, not speaking to each other. The agents are collaborating with nobody. The humans are collaborating with nobody.

Everyone is doing, in a shared space, the exact solo work they could have done at home, now with an uncomfortable chair and a commute attached.

I know this office because I have been there. I’ve worked as a fractional CPO at a variety of startups over the past few years and some of them required everyone in office for collaboration and culture purposes, and what was actually happening was a floor of people at open desks and shared tables, everyone heads-down in their own tasks, earbuds in, which is not collaborative in any way whatsoever.

The only real interaction occurred when somebody took a call out in the open and derailed the eight people near them, who were now straining to hear their own thoughts over somebody else’s pitch meeting. The in-person mandate had not created the intended collaboration. All it did was take solo work that people were doing fine at home and made it harder.

This is the part of “Office Space” that could have been a documentary. Peter Gibbons didn’t hate his job because the work was hard. He hated the commute, the eight bosses who each wanted the same TPS report, and the open floor where a man could lean over the partition at any moment to ask why he hadn’t used the new cover sheet.

The building added nothing to the work and did create a great deal of misery. The movie played it as absurd, but, frankly, a lot of return-to-office plans have adopted that as an operating model.

This is not an anecdote the research argues with. Ethan Bernstein and Stephen Turban put sensors on employees before and after a company tore out its walls for an open floor plan, the layout that is supposed to spark all that spontaneous mingling. Face-to-face interaction dropped by about seventy percent.

People responded to being shoved together by putting their headphones on and retreating into email and chat. This is the equivalent of throwing a party, forcing everyone to come, and watching them text each other from opposite corners of the room.

So if being in office isn’t producing collaboration, what is the mandate for? Yuye Ding and Mark Ma looked at the S&P 500 companies that ordered everyone back and found no improvement in firm value and a measurable drop in how people felt about the job. Their read was blunt. The mandates lined up with managers using the office to reassert control and to have someone to blame, not to get better work.

Forget the productivity numbers. The real cost is the people you lose, and you lose the best ones first.

Nicholas Bloom and his colleagues ran a real randomized trial, published in Nature, with more than sixteen hundred employees split between five days in and a hybrid schedule. The hybrid group quit about a third less often, with no hit to performance or promotions.

Forcing everyone back five days a week does not buy more output. It buys more resignations, and the first ones gone are the people with somewhere else to go.

That a pretty big cost for the privilege of watching your agents do the work in a room full of other people watching theirs.

The thing is, the people deepest into AI are the ones who most want to be together, and not to sit in silence. Janet Pogue McLaurin and her team at Gensler surveyed more than sixteen thousand workers and found that the heaviest AI users, about a third of everyone, are also the most collaborative, the most connected to their teams, and the most likely to come into the office. They are coming in for each other.

These five-day in-office mandates are coming almost entirely from the biggest companies, and, to be fair, that is the one place the evidence says in-person helps. Arpit Gupta, Abhinav Gupta, and Elena Simintzi tracked remote work across thousands of firms and found it cut productivity at established companies by about nine percent, while raising it at startups by about twelve.

Big, old organizations genuinely struggle to coordinate when scattered. Small teams thrive, because remote lets them hire the best people anywhere instead of the nearest people around. So the companies swinging the hardest mandates are the ones with a real coordination problem, and they are solving it by forcing the fix on everyone, including the small teams it only slows down.

What the room is actually for

Full disclosure. I have run my company fully remote since 2019, before the pandemic made it “cool.” For most of our work, I still think remote is the right answer. It’s not my favorite thing to admit that I have found that the office turns out to be very good at a few specific things, and that those few things are suddenly the only ones that really matter.

Once the agents take the production work, the part of the human’s job that remains relevant is to decide what’s worth making, to catch the thing that’s wrong and to teach the person above and below you on the ladder how to see it too.

That happens to be the work the research ties to being in a physical place together.

Melanie Brucks and Jonathan Levav ran a study putting pairs together either in person or over video and asking them to generate ideas. The in-person pairs came up with meaningfully more, and more creative, ideas. The video pairs were just as good at the next step, picking which idea to run with.

Basically, generating creative ideas is helped by sharing a space, and choosing the ones to implement isn’t. This lines up exactly with the split the agents just created. The machine is a fine partner for narrowing and deciding against known options. It is a worse one for the wide-open, slightly stupid, what-if-we-tried part, and that part goes better with a human across the table.

There is one finding that gives me pause, because it’s the real cost of how I’ve chosen to work, and it is definitely one AI has made worse.

Someone has to learn to do the actual jobs. People learn skills by sitting near other people who already know how, absorbing the small corrections, asking the dumb question out loud instead of filing a formal ticket for it. Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais measured this and found that junior engineers got dramatically more feedback when they sat near senior ones, and lost about a fifth of it when they went remote.

Proximity is how the craft gets handed down. Distance quietly starves it.

I feel this one personally, because it is the hardest part of running a company the way I do. One of my own designers, still growing in her career, put it this way. “Constructive feedback is how I know I’m improving, and that’s hard to get when you can’t just walk into your boss’s office and ask them to look at something with you. I’m lucky I’m on a small enough team that I feel comfortable reaching out. If I were part of anything larger, I think it would be much harder. Even on bigger client teams, the feedback I get from people outside my everyday group is thin, when I get it at all.”

She is right. The ambient coaching that used to just happen in a room, the over-the-shoulder correction, the pulled-aside-after-a-meeting, does not happen on its own when everyone is remote. We made it happen on purpose.

We hold a standing thirty-minute check-in every week, time that exists for nothing but the feedback and questions they’d otherwise have had to catch me in a hallway to ask. It is a deliberate, scheduled replacement for a thing that used to happen a bit more naturally. Remote turns the mentoring into something you have to build on purpose, instead of something you can assume.

This isn’t just happening at my company, of course. The KPMG American Worker Survey found AI adoption and office mandates rising together, and concluded that managers are now the linchpin for turning in-person time into real mentorship for the people earliest in their careers, the exact thing a crowded floor of people in headphones does not deliver on its own.

Now put that next to what the agents are doing. Remember the Stanford finding, that the entry-level jobs are the ones vanishing, because AI is doing the checkable, process-heavy tasks that used to be a junior’s whole first year. Those tasks were how you learned, by doing the boring version a hundred times until you could feel when it was wrong.

Anyone who watched Richie spend a week at that fine-dining restaurant on The Bear understands this. They hand him a mountain of forks to polish and nothing else, and he spends days furious about it, a grown man doing the most menial job in the building. Then somewhere in the repetition it clicks, and he comes out the other side understanding the whole craft in a way no shortcut could have taught him.

That was the art of apprenticeship. In our world, the agents are polishing the forks now, and the mentor who would have stood over you while you learned lives on a screen, if they’re there at all.

The on-ramp to every one of these careers is being pulled up from both ends at once, by the agents from below and by the distance from above, and almost nobody is talking about the two as the same problem. They are the same problem.

This is where the office earns its keep now, if it earns it anywhere. It’s not necessarily a place to produce deliverables, the agents clearly have that, but as the one place a person can still learn the judgment the agents can’t, from another person.

You cannot apprentice over a screen share nearly as well as you can over a shoulder.

Designers have already championed this work-style. Patrick Neeman has written that the next decade of design work is about owning the systems and the trade-offs underneath the screens, the part you can’t hand to a model. Vlad Derdeicea pointed out that most of a design lead’s day was never mired in pixels in the first place, but rather focusing on aligning, deciding, and convincing. Pushing pixels was a small piece of the day that a machine can now take, which gives leaders more time to do the teaching, which was always the actual job.

None of this adds up to an argument for the five-day in-office mandate. It adds up to something narrower. The office matters now for exactly the things it was never really designed to optimize, the idea you’d never have had alone, the greener team member who evolves by watching you work, the trust that only seems to set when people share a space. It matters more than ever, and for less than ever.

So what is the commute for

Every one of these mandates comes with the same justification. Andy Jassy wrote in his Amazon memo that collaborating, brainstorming, and inventing are simpler and more effective in person, and that teaching and learning from one another are more seamless. Jamie Dimon called the benefits of being together substantial and irreplaceable.

The reality is, these leaders are not wrong that those things matter, but it’s worth considering whether they are wrong that a mandate delivers them.

Chris Wardman describes this contradiction pretty bluntly, saying companies deploy AI that strips out the everyday interactions where knowledge actually transfers, then mandate attendance to protect the very thing they are automating away.

The Flex Index, which tracks the policies of roughly nine thousand companies, now puts about a third of American firms on full-time in-office, and the biggest companies are leading the charge. What that mostly creates, though, is a building full of people doing exactly the work that no longer needs a building. In the meantime, the collaboration they said they wanted is just sitting right there on the mandate, impossible to order up.

You cannot schedule serendipity for 9 a.m. Nobody mentors the new kid on command.

A good idea has never once shown up because a policy required it. Drag everyone in and chain them to the desks, and all you have manufactured is a more expensive version of the thing they were already doing at home, plus traffic.

A move that actually fits the current environment is narrower and a little strange. Treat the office the way you’d treat any specialized tool. You don’t run your whole life out of the one drawer with the good scissors, you open that drawer when you need the thing that’s in there.

Nicholas Bloom’s data keeps pointing at the same sweet spot, a couple of deliberate days together, the rest wherever the work actually gets done, which buys the retention and the output without the resentment.

Yuan Yuan and his colleagues found the same thing when looking at badge data from forty-three thousand people across a global company’s offices. Left alone, people coordinate their own in-person days around the work and the teammates that actually need to be there.

Any mandate that just counts heads on a Tuesday misses the point of being together. Come in for the ideation, the teaching, the arguing, the trust that only seems to set face to face. Then go home and let the agents run the production from a server farm that never needed to see your face anyway.

While the office technically never died, it shouldn’t be roaring back to what it was. AI merely changed what it’s for. For a hundred years it was where the work happened and now the work happens in the cloud, and the building is left holding the handful of human things we were always a little embarrassed to admit were the actual point.

Ryan Anderson, writing in Forbes about Atlassian’s internal findings, argues that as AI absorbs the routine work, value creation migrates toward the things that require human insight and collaboration, which makes the physical workplace more important, not less. Sure, AI doesn’t need an office, but the people using it do, mainly for the handful of things this quickly moving technology cannot do for them.

This brings us back to Alexa’s question. People are coming back to the office, but that was never really the question. The question is what they think they’re coming back to do. If the answer is to sit at a desk and quietly prompt a machine that works fine without them, next to other people doing the same, then they didn’t come back for the right reasons.

If people are merely driving in to be alone together, then, that, you really can do from home.

References and further reading

The work left the building

  • Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen, “Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts About the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence” (Stanford Digital Economy Lab, 2026). On the widening employment gap for young workers in AI-exposed jobs, as AI takes the entry-level tasks that once justified a first job.
  • Anthropic, “The Anthropic Economic Index.” Anthropic’s own analysis of how its models are used, with coding as the largest category and a large, growing share of use that automates tasks rather than assists.
  • Francisco Barrera Aros, “The crisis of the what” (UX Collective, 2026). A designer on AI taking over the how of building interfaces and coming for the what, leaving judgment as the differentiator.
  • Thomas Allen, “Managing the Flow of Technology” (MIT Press, 1977). The origin of the Allen Curve, the finding that communication between coworkers drops off sharply with physical distance.
  • Gartner, “Gartner Predicts 40% of Enterprise Apps Will Feature Task-Specific AI Agents by 2026” (2025). The forecast that agents built into software will jump from under five percent of enterprise apps to forty percent in a year.
  • Jose Maria Barrero, Nicholas Bloom and Steven J. Davis, “Why Working From Home Will Stick” (NBER, 2021). On the pandemic as a mass forced experiment in remote work, and how surprised workers were that they could do the job from home.

So everyone scattered, right?

  • Y Combinator, Frequently Asked Questions. YC’s own statement that the batch runs in person in San Francisco, having moved back after a brief remote stretch, because it works better that way.
  • Daniel Carmody, Martina Mazzarello, Paolo Santi and colleagues, “The effect of co-location on human communication networks” (MIT Senseable City Lab). On how remote work impedes the weak ties that form through physical proximity.
  • Mark Granovetter, “The Strength of Weak Ties” (American Journal of Sociology, 1973). The foundational work on why loose connections, not close ones, carry new information and ideas.
  • Janet Pogue McLaurin, Anita Grabowska and Katherine Engel, “Will AI Make the Workplace More Human?” (Gensler Global Workplace Survey 2026). A survey of more than sixteen thousand workers finding that the heaviest AI users are also the most collaborative, the most connected to their teams, and the most drawn to the office.

The office we actually built

  • Ethan Bernstein and Stephen Turban, “The impact of the ‘open’ workspace on human collaboration” (Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 2018). Sensor data showing face-to-face interaction fell about seventy percent after a move to open-plan.
  • Yuye Ding and Mark Ma, “Return-to-Office Mandates” (University of Pittsburgh). On RTO mandates at S&P 500 firms producing no gain in firm value, lower satisfaction, and higher turnover among skilled staff.
  • Nicholas Bloom, Ruobing Han and James Liang, “Hybrid working from home improves retention without damaging performance” (Nature, 2024). A randomized trial of 1,612 employees where hybrid work cut quit rates by a third with no hit to performance.
  • Arpit Gupta, Abhinav Gupta and Elena Simintzi, “Who Benefits from Remote Work?” (2025). On remote work raising productivity at startups while lowering it at established firms, based on data from thousands of companies.

What the room is actually for

  • Melanie Brucks and Jonathan Levav, “Virtual communication curbs creative idea generation” (Nature, 2022). In-person pairs generate more creative ideas than video pairs, who are just as good at selecting among them.
  • Natalia Emanuel, Emma Harrington and Amanda Pallais, “The Power of Proximity to Coworkers” (Quarterly Journal of Economics, 2026). Junior workers get far more feedback and mentorship when they sit near senior ones, and lose about a fifth of it when remote.
  • Patrick Neeman, “From faster pencil to AI Experience Architect” (UX Collective, 2026). On design work moving from making the screens to owning the systems and trade-offs a model can’t handle.
  • Vlad Derdeicea, “The 80% job: how design leads are using AI, and it’s not about mockups” (UX Collective, 2026). On most of a design lead’s work always being the human communication and judgment, with AI taking the production slice.

So what is the commute for

  • Andy Jassy, message to Amazon employees on returning to the office (2024). The Amazon CEO’s own stated reasons for the five-day mandate, collaboration, invention, and learning from one another in person.
  • Jamie Dimon, on JPMorgan’s return-to-office requirement. The CEO’s argument that the benefits of being together in person are substantial and irreplaceable.
  • The Flex Index (Scoop Technologies). The tracker of work-location policies across roughly nine thousand U.S. companies, showing about a third now require full-time in-office attendance.
  • Marie-Laure Charpignon, Yuan Yuan, and colleagues, “Navigating the new normal: Examining coattendance in a hybrid work environment” (PNAS, 2023). Badge data from forty-three thousand employees showing people coordinate their own in-person days around the work that needs it.
  • Ryan Anderson, “AI Is Making the Physical Workplace More Important, Not Less” (Forbes, 2026). On how, as AI absorbs routine work, value shifts to human collaboration and judgment, making the office more valuable for those things, drawing on Atlassian’s internal research.
  • Chris Wardman, “Companies Say Return-to-Office Mandates Are About Collaboration. Their AI Strategies Say Otherwise” (Built In, 2026). On the contradiction of mandating in-person work for collaboration while deploying AI that erodes the very interactions companies claim to want.
  • The KPMG American Worker Survey (2025). On rising AI adoption alongside rising return-to-office, and why managers are the linchpin for turning in-person time into mentorship for early-career workers.

title: What is a researcher’s worth?
text:
What is a researcher’s worth?

Why the debate over research isn’t a technology story – and why effortless AI makes human friction our scarcest asset.

We’re no stranger to this question.

For many years, research practitioners have talked with one another about how to “mature” teams so that they understand the value of our work in bringing success to their ventures. Or when we share the results of our research, we are peppered with questions about whether the findings are real, whether the methods are too weak or lack representativeness, or whether our subjects are even telling the truth when they express to us what they need.

But it’s not just research practitioners. Researchers in academia have been stripped of the funding they need to advance science. Academic departments have shuttered, and scholars’ voices have been dismissed as part of major civic scientific efforts, like the Census, the Environmental Protection Agency, or the Department of Education.

Put in this context, contemporary discourse around artificial intelligence replacing our jobs feels less like “the reason” than one reason among many when people question whether researchers (and research, in general) matter.

Over the last ten years, I’ve worked as an industry researcher while keeping a foot in academia, and have had some of the best work experiences of my life. There is a joy and a magic I find in what happens when you bring experts of different disciplines together – research, business, engineering, design, and more – to solve complex puzzles.

So if that cross-disciplinary magic is so real — and so productive — why do researchers in both companies and public life spend so much of their careers on the defensive? Most hot takes right now answer that question with new kinds of work: prompt faster, automate your synthesis, prove your return on investment.

As a social scientist, I think those takes miss what is actually happening. The debate over a researcher’s worth isn’t really a technology story. It’s a story about how institutions handle inconvenient truths.

Why institutions put research on trial.

Back in 2020, I wrote about one of my favorite scenes from the all-too-accurate show, Silicon Valley. In the episode, technologists watch through a one-way mirror as focus group participants give honest feedback about their app. One participant explained that the app made them feel “totally freaked out,” and another explained that it “made me feel stupid.”

Behind the mirror, the exec got angry. “Clearly none of these people get it, maybe this is a bad group…everyone that I showed the beta to loved it.” His colleague explained that this was the fifth focus group and they all shared the same feedback. She then realized he only gave the beta to his engineer friends. “I wanted to give it to people who would understand what I’m trying to do so I could get useful feedback,” he said. “And with all due respect, I gave it to you — the one person without a computing background – and you said it felt engineered.”

Those of us who love the craft of research love talking about research methods. But I find that in many cases, debates about methods in settings like these are not about finding what’s valuable. Methodological nitpicking is a way to avoid disruptions to a preferred plan. In this way, it is a shield against uncertainty – ironically, the very thing that research tries to disambiguate.

Social scientists argue that when under pressure, organizations gravitate toward commensuration – a process by which people working together flatten a messy, pluralistic set of realities into a single spreadsheet metric. The truth is, we do live in a world with a lot of unknowns, and the “winners” of today’s marketplace may not be the same in a few months or years. Under that uncertainty, it is tempting to flatten complex human behavior into click metrics – and flatten researchers into headcount cost compared against a chatbot – mistaking a tidy spreadsheet for certainty.

What AI actually changed: a mirror that rarely talks back.

In 2020, the lead technologist in Silicon Valley had to walk through the door and argue with human beings using their products. In 2026, they don’t have to do that anymore. They can swap the humans behind the glass for a synthetic AI persona trained to give feedback in specific ways.

I’m not here to say that AI is bad for science. I actually love a lot of the applications of artificial intelligence I get to use. I’m more troubled by the discourse around artificial intelligence and research in industry – how people talk about it – and the way it is compared to the human worth of social scientists.

For one, when organizations treat research as theater to rubber-stamp decisions they have already made, synthetic users and LLM summaries offer “good enough” reassurance at a fraction of the cost. Replacing hard-to-reach or marginalized communities with LLM agents doesn’t actually include them, either. It builds statistical caricatures out of dominant internet texts while erasing human consent and real-world inequities – the kind of blind spot that lets an automated camera “touch-up” feature quietly lighten darker skin tones if real people aren’t in the room.

And think about how culture actually moves. A few years ago, if you asked a model trained on historical averages what romance audiences wanted, it would tell you to center a man and a woman falling in love – it never would have bet on a breakout love story about two men playing hockey. Models fed past averages and synthetic data lose the tails of the distribution, the emerging subcultures and edge cases where the future actually starts. Meanwhile, algorithmic platforms mistake digital traces for human intent: a frustrated user clicking three times to fix a broken output looks like “high engagement” in behavioral logs.

Artificial intelligence is an interesting tool, not a good social scientist. But today, AI is giving anxious institutions the frictionless validation they secretly always wanted.

Looking in our own mirror.

Listen, I don’t think researchers are perfect by any means. We’re human after all! I actually think that researchers both in industry and academia accidentally made our worth easy to caricature.

Often professions survive or shrink based on what they claim jurisdiction over – what we diagnose problems to be, to what we attribute their causes, and how we offer treatment. In 2020, I warned that industry research was used too tactically (“go run a focus group”) as a way to drive impact. But over the last decade, much of industry research leaned into method gatekeeping – measuring our worth by how many people we interviewed or surveyed, or how many “insights” we delivered, or how many slide decks were shared.

At the same time, in academia, career incentives rewarded the world’s smartest experts for speaking mainly to peers behind journal paywalls rather than embedding social science into civic and institutional design. For example, a senior professor in my field asked me how I’d like the discipline to advance. I said that we should consider hiring clinical professors to more genuinely bring our findings to the field. He actually laughed at me. “Save it for social work,” he said.

I’m of the opinion that neither of these approaches has really helped anyone. In the former, we have traded using appropriate and defensible methods, asking big questions, and discussing complicated answers for a “study complete” checkbox. In the latter, we have siloed the magic of expert discovery almost entirely to the few people who read a published paper.

Where the magic of research lives.

Why does bringing research, engineering, design, and business together feel like magic? David Stark showed that breakthrough innovation happens in what he calls “heterarchies” – teams that hold competing accounts of worth in creative tension rather than collapsing everything into shipping speed. When AI coding tools let teams spin up twenty working prototypes in a week, velocity is no longer the scarce resource. Knowing which human dream is worth building becomes the scarcest asset in the room. For example, when do you pause a team buried in fifty usability bug fixes to instead ask whether we’re focused on the right value?

Some unfortunate news for my colleagues: humans don’t follow linear product models. They improvise inside their own social groups and cultural ecosystems. They react and adapt to major changes in their lives.

Engineers see systems; product managers see markets and funnels; and social scientists see social structure.

Social scientists can find and explain why youth culture over the last twenty years has shifted from public broadcasting to more intimate pockets of the internet. Or why a certain design aesthetic feels exciting in one region and troubling in another, shaped by the cultural meanings people there share. Or how chaotic-looking livestreams with tens of thousands of people are actually held together by the patterned, organized activities of moderators who keep conversation focused and fun.

In The Tacit Dimension, Hungarian-British polymath Michael Polanyi wrote that “we can know more than we can tell.” A vast amount of human knowledge is nonverbal. It includes how we think about cultural norms that we can’t summarize in a survey, or sometimes even in the context of an interview. My bet is that unguided LLMs can’t uncover that tacit knowledge on their own. But social scientists can. We triangulate methods and hold magnifying glasses up to a social problem in a variety of ways, including by testing our assumptions against an accumulated body of scholarly work in purposefully specific subfields.

Worth is built together.

Whether in a product sprint, a university lab, or a public agency, a researcher’s worth was never the focus group they run, how big or small their sample size is, or the paper they publish. Our worth is how we apply our training and our lens to the messy, plural, inconvenient realities of human life, even when institutions are tempted by easy mirrors that boil experience down to a lone metric.

To my research peers: bring your expertise and critical thinking to the work that you do. Show value to your teams by how you and your work “make the strange familiar, and the familiar strange” in the pursuit of a shared understanding grounded in human experience.

To my academic colleagues: get out of the ivory tower. Meet people who do research and engage in practice for purposes that have nothing to do with publishing. Learn new ways to talk about your work that shed both academic-ese and didactic habits in favor of two-way learning.

To my partners in research: resist the seduction of a mirror that always agrees with you. When AI makes spinning up twenty new ideas effortless, speed stops being your competitive edge – knowing what is actually true about people outside your building is. Invite the friction of someone trained to tell you when your favorite plan doesn’t match how humans really live.

We’ve spent years talking about how to “mature” organizations into valuing research, as if worth were a favor. It isn’t. Worth is built together.

Dr. Matt Rafalow is a senior staff researcher at YouTube, and a visiting scholar at University of Southern California. The views expressed in this article reflects the individual opinions of the author.
